Control, identification and experiments

Water-level regulation and performance optimisation

Francesco Ferri
9th semester · Water and Environment Engineering

Lecture 2 · 2 hours + 2-hour exercise

Ask how the quality of last week’s measurement affects today’s control decisions. The tank is the main worked example.

What you should be able to do

  • Identify the controlled output, manipulated input and disturbance.
  • Estimate a simple dynamic model from a step test.
  • Choose the correct feedback sign and tune a PI controller.
  • Compare designs using defined metrics and fair experiments.

Keep the focus on interpreting responses and making decisions. The exercise does not require deriving a general controller theory.

The lecture is 120 minutes including a ten-minute break. Use the optional slides only if there is time or as reading.

The measurement is part of the loop

  • The controller acts on the measured level.
  • Sensor bias can make the true level differ from the target.
  • Filtering reduces noise but adds dynamics.
  • Actuator limits restrict what the controller can achieve.

Connect directly to Lecture 1. Ask what a sensor reporting 2 cm too high would cause a level controller to do.

Source: System Control.pptx slide 5

The tank as a retention-pond model

VariableRole
Water level h [m]Controlled output
Outlet opening u, between 0 and 1Manipulated input
Inflow qᵢₙ [m³/s]Uncontrolled disturbance
Target level r [m]Reference

Here, a larger u means a more open outlet.

Do not change to an inlet-actuated tank halfway through the derivation. In a real pond, storage and downstream release constraints would also matter. This is a teaching model, not a pond design.

Which way should the valve move?

The measured level is above the target. Inflow is unchanged.

Should the outlet open or close?

Open. Increasing outflow removes water and lowers the level.

Give pairs a minute before revealing the answer. Open. Increasing outflow removes water and lowers the level.

Open loop and feedback

Open loop

  • Choose a valve opening.
  • Do not change it using the measured level.
  • An inflow change can shift the equilibrium.

Feedback

  • Measure the level repeatedly.
  • Compare it with the target.
  • Adjust the outlet to reduce the error.

A stable open-loop tank can still settle at the wrong level. Feedback is useful for disturbance rejection, not only for stabilising unstable systems.

Source: System Control.pptx slides 11–12

The feedback diagram

With e = r − h, the outlet-actuated tank requires the controller action to include a negative sign.

The diagram uses conventional reference-minus-output error. For the exercise we will instead define e_h = h-r and use positive gains. These are equivalent if the sign is handled consistently.

Source: System Control.pptx slides 18–19

Regulation, tracking and optimisation

ObjectiveExampleA useful metric
RegulationHold the level during an inflow changeIntegrated absolute level error
TrackingFollow a scheduled level targetTracking error and overshoot
OptimisationSelect WEC damping to increase absorbed powerMean absorbed power with limits

Regulation concerns disturbances around a reference. Tracking follows a changing reference. Optimisation requires specifying what is maximised and what constraints apply.

Source: System Control.pptx slides 18–23

Tank dynamics from mass conservation

$$A\frac{dh}{dt}=q_{\mathrm{in}}-q_{\mathrm{out}}$$
  • A is the constant horizontal area of the tank.
  • More inflow than outflow makes the level rise.
  • The level stores the history of the flow imbalance.

Assume incompressible water and constant tank area. A state is a minimal set of variables sufficient to predict future motion when inputs are known. Here the idealised plant state is h.

Source: Replaces the abstract hydraulic analogy in System Control.pptx slide 10

A gravity outlet

$$q_{\mathrm{out}}=C_d a_{\max}u\sqrt{2gh}=k u\sqrt h$$
$$A\dot h=q_{\mathrm{in}}-k u\sqrt h$$

Assumptions: free discharge, negligible downstream head, and opening proportional to effective outlet area.

Here k=C_d a_max sqrt(2g), with units m^(5/2)/s. Real valves may have a nonlinear opening characteristic, delay and hysteresis. A gravity outlet couples level and outflow.

Source: System Control.pptx slide 35, nonlinear-valve context

Equilibrium and feasibility

$$q_{\mathrm{in},0}=k u_0\sqrt{h_0}$$
$$u_0=\frac{q_{\mathrm{in},0}}{k\sqrt{h_0}}$$

A steady target needs an opening within the available range: 0 ≤ u₀ ≤ 1.

If inflow exceeds the fully open outlet capacity at the target level, no controller can hold that target. Similarly, closing an outlet cannot actively fill an empty tank without inflow.

A numerical teaching model

ParameterValue
Tank area A0.05 m²
Initial / nominal level h₀0.30 m
Nominal inflow q₀1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³/s = 6 L/min
Nominal opening u₀0.50
Outlet coefficient k3.6515 × 10⁻⁴ m⁵ᐟ²/s

Nominal stored volume: A h₀ = 15 L.

These values are chosen for the simulation exercise and are not measurements of the lab tank. They give plausible slow dynamics and a convenient equilibrium.

Local linear behaviour

$$h=h_0+\Delta h,\quad u=u_0+\Delta u$$
$$A\Delta\dot h=\Delta q_{\mathrm{in}}-\frac{q_0}{2h_0}\Delta h-\frac{q_0}{u_0}\Delta u$$

Small changes near an operating point can be approximated by a linear model.

The derivatives of k*u*sqrt(h) are q0/(2h0) with respect to h and q0/u0 with respect to u. Do not ask students to memorise the expression. Emphasise that the model depends on the operating point.

A first-order tank model

$$G_u(s)=\frac{\Delta H(s)}{\Delta U(s)}=\frac{K}{\tau s+1}$$
$$K=-\frac{2h_0}{u_0}=-1.2\ \mathrm{m},\qquad\tau=\frac{2Ah_0}{q_0}=300\ \mathrm s$$

The negative gain records a physical fact: opening the outlet lowers the level.

K is metres per unit opening. An increase in u of 0.01 gives about -0.012 m at steady state locally. The same first-order form appeared in the RC filter. Transfer functions describe perturbations with zero initial perturbation.

System identification

Estimate a model from measured input and output data.

  • Choose the operating point and the model purpose.
  • Apply a known, informative input change.
  • Record the actual input and output with timestamps.
  • Fit on one record and validate on another.

The input must vary enough to reveal the dynamics above the noise. Inflow variation during a valve test is a disturbance that can bias the identified model.

Source: System Control.pptx slide 34

A step test

  • Start from a steady level and opening.
  • Apply a modest change in outlet opening.
  • Hold the opening long enough to observe the new level.
  • Keep inflow fixed in simulation, or measure its variation.
  • Repeat with a separate input change for validation.

For this simulation use an opening change of +0.02. Do not confuse a commanded valve change with the actual valve position if actuator dynamics matter. A physical test would need equipment-specific limits.

Reading gain and time constant

$$K\approx\frac{h_\infty-h_0}{u_1-u_0}$$
$$h(t)=h_0+K\Delta u\left(1-e^{-(t-L)/\tau}\right),\quad t\ge L$$

After the delay L, the response reaches 63.2% of its total change in one time constant τ.

Use the final change with its sign. For a falling response, 63.2 percent means 63.2 percent down toward the final level. Estimate the delay before estimating tau. The exercise model has no pure delay.

Worked step-test estimate

Opening changes from 0.50 to 0.52. Level changes from 0.300 m to about 0.2774 m.

$$K_{\mathrm{est}}\approx\frac{0.2774-0.300}{0.02}\approx-1.13\ \mathrm{m}$$
$$h_{63\%}\approx0.300+0.632(0.2774-0.300)=0.2857\ \mathrm m$$

The crossing occurs approximately 280 s after the step.

The finite-step estimate differs slightly from the local linear gain because the plant is nonlinear. Exact equilibrium is 0.3*(0.5/0.52)^2 = 0.277367 m. The 63 percent time is about 281 s in the ideal nonlinear simulation. The plotted or logged data should support the estimate.

The identified step response

The response is computed from the nonlinear gravity-outlet equation. The final level is 0.27737 m. The 63.2 percent crossing is about 281 s after the opening change. Read the time from the instant of the step, not from the start of the record.

Source: Numerical integration of the teaching equations and stated parameters.

Validation on a different step

  • Use the fitted model to predict a second record.
  • Compare the sign, final change and response speed.
  • Plot measured minus predicted level.
  • Look for persistent structure in the residual.

Do not fit and validate on the same trace. A model can match one step and fail elsewhere. For the exercise, use an opening change from 0.50 to 0.48 as the second record.

Check: an unexplained level rise

During an outlet-opening step test, the level rises. Could this mean the valve has positive gain?

Possibly, but first check the opening convention, actual valve motion, sensor sign and inflow. A changing disturbance can hide the valve’s effect.

Give pairs a minute before revealing the answer. Possibly, but first check the opening convention, actual valve motion, sensor sign and inflow. A changing disturbance can hide the valve’s effect.

Proportional control with a clear sign

$$e_h=h-r$$
$$u_{\mathrm{cmd}}=u_0+K_p e_h,\qquad K_p>0$$

If the level is too high, eₕ is positive and the outlet opens. If it is too low, the outlet closes.

We now consistently use measured-minus-reference error. Kp has units 1/m. An equivalent implementation using r-h requires negative gains or an explicit sign reversal.

Source: System Control.pptx slides 24–27

Why P control leaves an offset

At the original level, a larger constant inflow needs a larger outlet opening.

A P controller can produce that extra opening only while a non-zero error remains.

$$\Delta h_{\mathrm{ss}}=\frac{\Delta q_{\mathrm{in}}}{q_0/(2h_0)+(q_0/u_0)K_p}$$

This equation follows from the linear steady balance. For Kp=2 1/m and a 20 percent inflow increase, the local error is about 0.0353 m. This offset claim is specific to the chosen plant and bias.

Source: System Control.pptx slide 27

Integral action

$$u_{\mathrm{cmd}}=u_0+K_p e_h+K_i\int e_h\,dt$$

A persistent error changes the integral contribution until the required opening is reached.

At equilibrium, the error can return to zero while the integral contribution remains non-zero.

Ki has units 1/(m s). A stable, unsaturated PI loop can reject a constant disturbance with zero steady-state error in this ideal model. Sensor bias still matters.

Source: System Control.pptx slides 25–28

Derivative action

$$u_D=K_d\frac{dh}{dt}$$
  • Responds to the rate of change of the measured output.
  • Can help shape fast dynamics.
  • Amplifies high-frequency measurement noise unless filtered.
  • For this slow tank exercise, start with PI.

With our h-r convention, a positive rate of level rise should increase opening. Derivative on measurement avoids a derivative kick from a reference step. D does not eliminate steady-state offset.

Source: System Control.pptx slide 29

Break

10 minutes

After the break: actuator limits, performance measures and fair comparisons.

Return at minute 70.

Saturation

$$u=\min\left(1,\max(0,u_{\mathrm{cmd}})\right)$$

The controller can request an impossible opening. The actuator cannot provide it.

Example: at h = 0.30 m, the fully open outlet passes 12 L/min in the teaching model.

The maximum flow is k*sqrt(0.3) = 0.0002 m3/s. If inflow is above this, the level initially rises even at full opening. Saturation makes the closed loop nonlinear.

Integral windup

  • The controller reaches an opening limit.
  • The error persists and the integral continues to grow.
  • When conditions change, the integral may take a long time to recover.

Anti-windup: stop integration when it would push the command farther beyond its limit.

Clamping and back-calculation are standard implementations. In the exercise code, clamping uses the actual total command, including the nominal bias. Integral updates that move the command back toward the valid range remain allowed.

Source: MathWorks: https://www.mathworks.com/help/simulink/slref/anti-windup-control-using-a-pid-controller.html

A practical tuning sequence

  • Verify the controller sign with a small disturbance.
  • Set integral action to zero and choose a modest P gain.
  • Increase P only while the response remains acceptable.
  • Add slow integral action to remove the remaining offset.
  • Test limits, measurement noise and another operating condition.

Do not deliberately seek sustained oscillation on the lab apparatus. Tuning tendencies are not universal laws. A delay, valve dynamics or noisy measurement can change the result.

Source: Revised from System Control.pptx slides 30–33

An optional model-based starting point

For a first-order model with gain K < 0, negligible delay, and eₕ = h − r:

$$K_p=\frac{\tau}{|K|\lambda},\qquad T_i=\tau,\qquad K_i=\frac{K_p}{T_i}$$
$$\lambda=150\ \mathrm s\quad\Rightarrow\quad K_p=1.67\ \mathrm{m^{-1}},\quad K_i=0.00556\ \mathrm{(m\,s)^{-1}}$$

A larger λ gives a slower starting design. Validate on the nonlinear model.

This is a first-order pole-cancellation design, not a general formula for delayed or nonlinear plants. The controller cancels the model pole ideally and leaves a target closed-loop time constant lambda. The chosen values are a starting point, not a promised optimum.

Response measures

  • Rise time: often 10% to 90% of a reference step.
  • Overshoot: excursion beyond the target.
  • Settling time: time to remain inside a specified band.
  • Steady-state error: final target deviation.

The original image is a generic positive reference step. For inflow disturbance rejection, use maximum level deviation, recovery time and integrated error. Specify the settling band in metres where possible.

Source: System Control.pptx slide 14

Comparing tank controllers

$$\mathrm{IAE}=\int_0^T|h(t)-r(t)|\,dt$$
MetricMeaning
IAE [m·s]Total level deviation over a defined window
Maximum |h − r| [m]Worst excursion
Total variation of uValve activity
Time at limits [s]Demand that reaches actuator bounds

Use the same initial condition, disturbance and integration window for all controllers. A smaller IAE may require excessive valve motion. There is no universally best controller without priorities.

P and PI under the same inflow change

Teaching-model simulation. Inflow rises 20 percent at 300 s. Kp=2 for both curves, Ki=0 for P and 0.005 for PI. P approaches a nonzero offset. PI is still recovering at 1200 s: an 8.1 mm error at the end is a transient residual, not its theoretical steady-state error. The post-disturbance IAE values are approximately 27.92 and 15.98 m s.

Source: Numerical integration of the teaching equations and stated parameters.

Stability and realistic limits

  • A stable response remains bounded under bounded inputs.
  • Sustained or growing oscillation needs investigation.
  • Linear pole locations test the local model.
  • Saturation, delays and operating-point changes need simulation or tests.

For a proper minimal continuous-time rational transfer function, BIBO stability requires all poles strictly in the left half-plane. Poles on the imaginary axis do not imply BIBO stability. Do not use the source definition requiring convergence to a constant for every bounded input.

Source: Corrects System Control.pptx slide 15

Design of experiments

A test plan connects a question to measurements that can answer it.

PartTank example
QuestionDoes integral action improve disturbance rejection?
FactorP versus PI controller
ResponseIAE and maximum level deviation
Conditions to controlInitial level and imposed inflow change

Write the question before running the simulation. A large amount of data does not compensate for changing several uncontrolled conditions.

Source: System Control.pptx slides 38–41

Factors, levels and interactions

Two factors: controller type and disturbance size.

Run conditionControllerInflow increase
1P10%
2PI10%
3P30%
4PI30%

An interaction means that the effect of PI depends on disturbance size.

This is a 2-by-2 factorial design. Randomise actual run order when appropriate. In deterministic simulation, repetitions with identical inputs give no new information. Vary noise realisations if studying noise effects.

Source: System Control.pptx slides 39–44

Replication, randomisation and blocking

  • Replication: repeat independent trials to estimate variation.
  • Randomisation: vary test order to reduce confounding with drift.
  • Blocking: compare settings within similar conditions, such as one wave record or one day.

A thousand samples in one run are not a thousand independent experiments. For WEC simulations, using the same wave record for paired comparisons can reduce noise in the difference. Use additional records to test generalisation.

Source: System Control.pptx slides 40–42

Power and energy in a WEC

$$P_{\mathrm{abs}}(t)=-F_{\mathrm{PTO}}(t)\,v(t)$$
$$E_{\mathrm{abs}}=\int_0^T P_{\mathrm{abs}}(t)\,dt,\qquad\bar P=E_{\mathrm{abs}}/T$$

FPTO is the PTO force on the body, along the velocity coordinate.

The sign convention matters. A resisting force has opposite sign to velocity, so absorbed power is positive. Force times velocity is watts, not joules. Electrical output differs because of conversion losses. This is context, not a lab protocol.

Source: Corrects System Control.pptx slide 21

Damping and mean absorbed power

$$F_{\mathrm{PTO}}=-b_{\mathrm{PTO}}v\quad\Rightarrow\quad P_{\mathrm{abs}}=b_{\mathrm{PTO}}v^2$$

Increasing damping also changes velocity. Therefore, more damping does not necessarily produce more mean power.

Compare mean absorbed power under matched waves and the same force and motion limits.

This relation assumes an ideal viscous PTO. The speed is not independent of damping. Excessive damping can suppress motion. Avoid claiming a universal optimal damping without a model or measurements.

Source: System Control.pptx slides 7–8, 21

A fair optimisation comparison

  • Define the response: mean absorbed power over a fixed steady window.
  • Change the damping setting across a stated range.
  • Use matched wave conditions for each comparison.
  • Repeat with independent wave records and report variation.
  • Check force and motion limits before ranking settings.

A single best run can reflect favourable waves. Separate the data used to choose a setting from the data used to evaluate it. Measurement phase mismatch between force and velocity can bias power.

Source: System Control.pptx slides 38–44

Check: is controller B better?

Controller A and B use different wave records. B produces 8% more mean power in one run.

What can you conclude?

B produced more power in those runs. A controller advantage is not yet isolated. Use matched comparisons, independent repeats and uncertainty estimates.

Give pairs a minute before revealing the answer. B produced more power in those runs. A controller advantage is not yet isolated. Use matched comparisons, independent repeats and uncertainty estimates.

Two-hour exercise

Exercise: tank control in Simulink

Identify the tank response, implement feedback and compare P with PI.

  • Use the supplied ideal nonlinear tank model.
  • Document the error convention and control sign.
  • Keep all simulation parameters and test windows with the results.

This is a separate two-hour exercise. The MATLAB builder creates the Simulink model. It includes plant, reference, disturbance, a controller subsystem and logging. Students edit the controller function and settings.

Two-hour exercise

Exercise timing

MinutesTask
0–15Open model and confirm equilibrium
15–40Identify a step-response model
40–55Validate with a different step
55–80Implement and tune P then PI
80–105Compare disturbance rejection and saturation
105–120Submit plots, metrics and conclusions

If model setup is slow, supply the built model before class. The builder and a MATLAB-only simulation are included. The latter provides a fallback without Simulink.

Two-hour exercise

Exercise 1: equilibrium and sign

  • Run the tank at u = 0.50 and inflow 6 L/min.
  • Confirm h remains at 0.30 m.
  • Increase u to 0.52 and explain the direction of the response.
  • Estimate the new steady level using the nonlinear balance.

Expected steady level is 0.27737 m. If the level increases, inspect the sign convention or wiring of model blocks. This check comes before controller tuning.

Two-hour exercise

Exercise 2: identification

  • Use the step at t = 100 s and run to 2000 s.
  • Estimate K and τ from the recorded opening and level.
  • Predict the response to an opening step from 0.50 to 0.48.
  • Compare the prediction with a new simulation.

The exact second equilibrium is 0.32552 m. A local linear model predicts about 0.324 m. Small differences are expected due to nonlinearity. Use the identification_demo script for the plotting framework.

Two-hour exercise

Exercise 3: P and PI

  • Choose eₕ = h − r. Start with Kₚ = 2 m⁻¹ and Kᵢ = 0.
  • Apply a 20% inflow increase at t = 300 s.
  • Record the final error and valve opening.
  • Add Kᵢ = 0.005 (m·s)⁻¹ as a starting point.
  • Adjust the gains and justify the final choice.

Use a 1200-second run. Starting values are deliberately modest, not optimal. Students should see the P offset and PI recovery. The supplied controller file initially implements P. The guide explains how to add the integral term.

Two-hour exercise

Exercise 4: limits and fair comparison

  • Run the same 1200 s test for the selected P and PI designs.
  • Compare IAE, maximum deviation and valve activity over 300–1200 s.
  • Apply a temporary 150% inflow increase to expose saturation.
  • Compare PI recovery with and without anti-windup.
  • State one limitation of the model.

The saturation test raises inflow to 2.5 times nominal from 300 to 600 s. This temporarily exceeds maximum outflow at the target. It illustrates windup and capacity. Do not interpret this simulation as a physical test instruction.

Two-hour exercise

What to submit

  • One plot for identification and one for independent validation.
  • Level and opening traces for P and PI under the same disturbance.
  • A short table of gains and performance metrics.
  • The sign convention, anti-windup logic and a short conclusion.
  • The model or code needed to reproduce the results.

A successful answer should explain why the outlet opens when level rises, why P leaves offset, and why a controller cannot overcome a capacity limit.

Optional material

Optional: feedback transfer functions

Using conventional e = r − h:

$$C(s)=-\left(K_p+\frac{K_i}{s}\right),\qquad G(s)=\frac{K}{\tau s+1}$$
$$\frac{H(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{G(s)C(s)}{1+G(s)C(s)}$$

Both G and C have negative static action, so their loop product has the intended feedback sign.

Use perturbation variables. This expression assumes unity measurement feedback and no saturation. A sensor filter would enter the loop model.

Source: System Control.pptx slides 26, 36–37

Optional material

Optional: mechanical analogy

$$M\ddot x+B\dot x+K_xx=F$$
$$\frac{X(s)}{F(s)}=\frac{1}{Ms^2+Bs+K_x}$$

For a simplified WEC oscillator, hydrodynamic coefficients and excitation complicate the real dynamics. This is an analogy for energy storage and damping, not a complete WEC model.

Source: System Control.pptx slides 7–8

Optional material

Optional: more informative identification

  • A chirp excites a range of frequencies.
  • PRBS and multisine inputs can also reveal dynamics.
  • Choose amplitude, bandwidth and duration for the model purpose.

The image illustrates the principle. Do not identify numerical parameters from this small source figure. Step tests are sufficient for the introductory tank exercise.

Source: System Control.pptx slide 34

Optional material

Optional: model predictive control

  • Predict candidate future responses with a model.
  • Optimise a defined objective under constraints.
  • Apply the first action and repeat with new measurements.

MPC is a possible later extension for release limits or WEC objectives. Its performance depends on the model, state estimates and optimisation. PID should not be labelled state-based in contrast to MPC.

Source: System Control.pptx slides 16, 22–23
